20.23.13.en: Sts. Barsanuphius and John v "Presents and gifts blind the eyes of the wise" (see Sir 20:29), and he who accepts them to cause harm to others is not an ascetic.

20.24.0.en: Counsels for the ascetics by St. Hyperechius the priest Wisdom that is hid and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both? [30]

20.24.1.en: v Those who are able to teach with great effect but who keep away because of excessive humility ought to learn, by reasoning from the consideration of small things, how greatly they sin against the greater and more important duties. Therefore, if they hide from needy brethren the money they have, they undoubtedly spread gloom and sorrow among them. Let them reflect in how great a guilt they are involved, because they withhold the word of teaching from sinful brethren, withholding the medicine of life from souls walking toward death. Therefore the wise man says truly: "Wisdom that is hid and treasure that is hoarded up, what profit is in them both?" (see Sir 20:32). If a famine were to come that destroyed a people, and the people hid their wheat, these would without doubt be heralds and preachers of death. Therefore let those who do not come forward to serve the bread of grace that has been bestowed on them consider, when souls perish from thirst for the holy word, how great the terror of the punishment will be. For this reason it was also truly said by the tongue of Solomon: "He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him" (Prov 11:26); he who hides the wheat monopolizes for himself the words of holy teaching. Such a man is struck by the curse, because by the sin of silence he deserves the punishment of all those who could have walked in what is right because of him [29].

20.25.0.en: The man who hides his folly is better than the man who hides his wisdom [31].

20.25.1.en: Let a man hide his folly by his silence; this is better than he who hides his wisdom.

20.26.s.en: Let me cling to You in my silence as in my words!

20.26.0.en: v What occupies me in my silence as in my speech is clinging to You!

20.26.1.en: In my silence I enter into a secret conversation with You, and with my words I speak according to Your direction for me.

20.26.2.en: You speak through me, so I bear a spirit of love and long-suffering even toward those who trouble me.

20.26.3.en: Grant me not to speak in a spirit of folly. Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a strong door over my lips.

20.26.4.en: v Grant me the spirit of wisdom, lest a temporary success draw me to haughtiness.

20.26.5.en: Let me not rejoice in temporal gains that turn into losses, nor seek the glory of the world, for You are my glory.

20.26.6.en: v I ask nothing of the fool, lest he count me as his debtor.

20.26.7.en: He gives me today, and takes from me double!

20.26.8.en: Remove from me all folly, for what occupies me is Your friendship toward me.

20.26.9.en: Train me in conversation with You, that my soul may be satisfied with Your love!

20.26.10.en: Train my tongue, that I may not fall into a slip of the tongue, but let my words be seasoned with the salt of the Spirit; Your grace lifts me up, so that I speak only what I taste and live!

20.26.11.en: v Grant me wisdom, that I may not give promises that I am unable to fulfill!

20.26.12.en: Let all my promises and words be true, for You are the Truth and the Life!

20.26.13.en: Grant me not to steal what is not mine.

20.26.14.en: v Let every word that comes out of my mouth proclaim Your righteousness.

20.26.15.en: Let me know when to speak with wisdom and when to be silent.

21.0.s.en: 1. Flee from sin in a spirit of hope

21.0.0.en: 1 My son, hast thou sinned? do so no more, but ask pardon for thy former sins. 2 Flee from sin as from a serpent; for if thou comest near it, it will bite thee. 3 Its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, slaying the souls of men. 4 All iniquity is as a two-edged sword, the wound whereof cannot be healed.

21.0.1.en: My son, have you sinned? Do not add to it, but pray concerning your former sins [1].

21.0.2.en: Sin has gained mastery over humanity, because it isolated itself from God, the source of holiness and purity, and so it became in need of the spirit of hope, the giver of joy. Sometimes a man walks for a certain period in a spirit of chastity and purity, and suddenly he is fought by an evil thought or a bad lust or the practice of some sin, and he thinks that he has lost his purity completely, and instead of returning to God he surrenders to sins. Therefore Ben Sira says: "My son, hast thou sinned? Do so no more, but pray concerning thy former sins."

21.0.3.en: He addresses his speech to the sinner, saying: "My son"; for in wishing to instill a spirit of hope in the sinner he counts him as his son, that he may see in him the image of God his Father. He calls him to prayer in a spirit of hope together with earnestness, instead of surrendering to sin.

21.0.4.en: v When the soul understands sin, it hates it, (and looks at it) as a wild beast of foul smell. But when the soul is ignorant of sin, sin becomes beloved to it, and enslaves the soul that loves it and takes it captive. The wretched poor man does not see what is able to save him, nor does he even think of this, but welcomes sin with pleasure, imagining that it adorns him [1].

21.1.0.en: v The pure soul is sanctified and enlightened by God because of its clarity. Then its mind thinks of what is good, and good inclinations and deeds spring from it. But the soul that is defiled by sin, God abandons it, or rather it is the one that leaves Him, and so it lets evil demons into its thought, and they suggest (to its owner) shameful things: fornication, murder, robbery and other similar evil and demonic deeds [2].

21.1.1.en: St. Anthony the Great v Remember these things, that with them you may stop the mouths of the lazy, the immoral, the slack and those who hate works of virtue, those who accuse the Master of all. You have sinned. Be silent; but "hast thou sinned? Do so no more." For there is no sin worse than that after you sin you accuse the Master. Know the cause of sin and you will find that no one sinned but you. In every position there is need of a good intention. And I show you this not by reasoning only, but by examples from your fellow servants who walk in this same world. Use this means also...

21.1.2.en: Is someone a fornicator? Present to him another man who is self-controlled.

21.1.3.en: Is someone covetous and greedy? Show him a man who gives alms.

21.1.4.en: Does he live in jealousy and envy? Make known to him a man who is pure of this pain.

21.2.0.en: Is he overcome by anger? Bring into the midst a man who walks in wisdom [3].

21.2.1.en: St. John Chrysostom v To cease from sin is not enough, if we neglect the correction of the old offense. Holy Scripture says: "My son, hast thou sinned? Do so no more!" But lest you think that this alone is safe, he hastened to say concerning the past: "Pray concerning thy former sins" [1]. But what benefit is there in such prayer, if you are not qualified to have your prayer heard because there are no fruits meet for repentance, lest you be cut down like a tree without fruit and cast into the fire (Mt 25:42). If you wish your prayer concerning your sins to be heard: "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven" (Lk 6:37) [4].

21.3.0.en: v In truth repentance for sins reforms men, but it shows no benefit if it is barren of works of mercy. This is what the Truth bears witness to by the tongue of John, who said to those who came to him: "O generation of vipers, who hath warned you to flee from the wrath to come? Bring forth therefore fruits worthy of repentance, and begin not to say within yourselves, We have Abraham to our father: for I say unto you, that God is able of these stones to raise up children unto Abraham. And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: every tree therefore which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire" (Lk 3:7-9).. The multitudes asked him, saying: "What shall we do then?" He answered and said unto them: "He that hath two coats, let him impart to him that hath none; and he that hath meat, let him do likewise"... What does this mean except what those on the left hear: "Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: for I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat" (Mt 25:41-42).. And what will it profit you if you ask forgiveness without preparing yourselves to be heard, by not bringing forth "fruits worthy of repentance," so that you are cut down like a tree without fruit and cast into the fire? If you wish to be heard when you ask forgiveness, "Forgive, and ye shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given unto you" (Lk 6:37-38) [5].

21.4.0.en: St. Augustine v Some not only do not repent of what they do, but they support their (evil) conduct without ceasing and approve of it. Truly the sin that is supported is multiplied. Rightly one condemns this attitude by saying: "My son, hast thou sinned? Add not to what thou hast done." He adds sin upon sin who adds to what he has done a justification of his fault.. So when Adam, the first man, was asked about his fault.. God's question to him was a call to repentance, but Adam answered justifying himself, saying: "The woman whom thou gavest to be with me, she gave me of the tree, and I did eat" (Gen 3:12). Adam blames his Creator by implication for his falling into disobedience. It is as though Adam were saying: "You provided me with an opportunity to commit sin, because You gave me the woman." This kind of sin remains evident in the human race to the present time. We still justify our sinful acts [6].

21.4.2.en: Flee from sin as you flee from a serpent, for if you come near it, it will bite you.

21.4.3.en: Its teeth are as the teeth of a lion, destroying the souls of men [2].

21.4.4.en: The man who is sincere in his repentance, when he sins, immediately resorts to God in prayer seeking forgiveness, looking at sin as a deadly poison, fleeing from it as from the venom of the serpent with the teeth of a lion. The strength of the penitent is in not conversing with sin as Eve did with the serpent; for fleeing from sin is not cowardice but has in it courage, strength and wisdom. The Apostle says: "Flee fornication" (1 Cor 6:18).

21.4.5.en: He speaks here of the enemy of good who seduces us to surrender to sins, likening him to a serpent with teeth like the teeth of a lion; for Satan fought Eve by the tongue of the serpent, and Peter looked at the enemy of good as a roaring lion walking about seeking whom he may devour (Gen 3:1-7; 1 Pet 5:8).

21.5.0.en: v Sin is the unclean thing; let us flee from it and abstain from it. "If thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2).. What does it not defile? It defiles the hands and the soul, the very house in which we place the evil treasure. Yet the Jews counted this as nothing. Moses carried the bones of Joseph (which in the eyes of the Jews were unclean), and Samson drank from the jawbone of an ass and ate honey from the lion, and Elijah was fed by ravens. Tell me, if we hold these things dear, what is more unclean than our books made of the skins of (dead) animals? [7]

21.6.0.en: v It befits us not to confine ourselves to the outward form and the shadows, but to draw near to the truth and hold fast to it. Sin is an unclean thing. "If thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2) [8].

21.7.0.en: v Let us avoid every sin completely, for because of it He is blasphemed. It is said: "Flee from sin as from a serpent, for if thou comest near it, it will bite thee" (see Sir 21:2). It does not come to us, but we are the ones who seek it [9].

21.7.1.en: St. John Chrysostom All iniquity is as a two-edged sword, and there is no healing for its wound [3].

21.7.2.en: Iniquity is rebellion; the Lord says of it that it is a man's doing what is right in his own eyes (Deut 12:8). If sin is like a two-edged sword, our salvation requires the Word of God, which is like a two-edged sword (Heb 4:13).

21.8.0.en: 5 Terror and violence will waste riches: thus the house of the proud shall be made desolate. 6 A prayer out of a poor man's mouth reacheth to the ears of God, and his judgment cometh speedily. 7 He that hateth to be reproved is in the way of sinners, but he that feareth the Lord will repent from his heart. 8 An eloquent man is known afar off; but a man of understanding knoweth when he slippeth. 9 He that buildeth his house with other men's money is like one that gathereth himself stones for the tomb of his burial. 10 The congregation of the wicked is like tow wrapped together: and the end of them is a flame of fire to destroy them. 11 The way of sinners is made plain with stones, but at the end thereof is the pit of hell.

21.8.1.en: After calling us to flee from sin in general, he concentrated on the fall of the rich into wronging the poor, and the fall into pride of those who think themselves godly or rich in virtue. It befits the unjust and the proud not to hate rebuke but to fear, so that they return to the Lord with their hearts. But the danger into which the wicked fall is their clinging to one another, so that their hearts grow content with evil, and one draws the other to descend further into the flame of the fire of hell.

21.8.2.en: If the gate of truth is narrow and its way hard, then the way of sin is wide and paved with smooth stones; once someone slips on it he cannot stand, but descends without stopping. He needs the grace of God, which supports him in keeping the divine commandment and plants in him the fear of the Lord. By this he takes control of his thoughts and enjoys the divine wisdom.

21.8.3.en: Terror and violence destroy wealth, and likewise the house of the proud is destroyed [4].

21.8.4.en: God does not accept violence and injustice, and even rejects the alms of the violent and unjust man.

21.8.5.en: v Why do you revile the Lord by offering Him unclean sacrifices and gifts?!... It is better for you not to strip some men in order to clothe others; do you not wrong those whom you strip? For if you wrong them, even if you give to others what you took from them, this is not mercy.

21.8.6.en: v If you seize money and give it to others... what is your excuse? Do you want to know the measure of the evil you do? Hear what Solomon says, that he who offers a sacrifice from the goods of the poor is like one who kills a son before his father!

21.8.7.en: St. John Chrysostom v Enough, O rich man, you have forgotten your formation; let not temporal wealth, which does not save you, deceive you.

21.8.8.en: O mighty and strong one, rebuke yourself; why do you threaten, when if your heart forgets the Lord, you are weak?

21.8.9.en: True is the word of prophecy: let not the wise man, nor the mighty, nor the rich man boast.

21.9.0.en: Let a man boast in the Lord, if he boasts, for he abides forever; to Him be praise [10].

21.9.1.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh The prayer of the poor goes out of his mouth, and reaches the ears of the Lord, and quickly his judgment is executed for him [5].

21.9.2.en: God is the God of the poor and the oppressed and those who have no one to ask after them; He inclines His ears to all the suffering, needy and forgotten, and hears the cries of their hearts. He is overcome by their prayers, their sighs and their tears; He says to them: "Turn away thine eyes from me, for they have overcome me" (Song 6:5).

21.9.3.en: v Prayer alone is what overcomes God (for He is merciful). But the Lord Christ affirmed that it does not work on behalf of evil, and He gave it all its power when it is used for good. It knows only to give strength to the weak, to heal the sick, to loose those bound by evil spirits, to open the bars of prisons, and to loose the bonds of the righteous.

21.9.4.en: It also washes away faults and restrains temptations, and extinguishes the fires of persecution, and comforts faint souls, and encourages the downcast, and guides travelers, calms the waves, frightens robbers, refreshes the poor, and restrains the rich.

21.9.5.en: Prayer raises those who are going down, saves those who have fallen, and establishes those who stand.

21.10.0.en: Prayer is the wall of the faith. It arms us and shoots arrows toward the enemy who lies in wait for us on every side. So we shall not be unarmed. By day we are aware of our duty, and by night of our watching. And bearing the weapon of prayer we guard the banner of our Commander. And we wait in prayer for the trumpet of the archangel [11].

21.10.1.en: The scholar Tertullian He who hates rebuke walks in the steps of the sinner, but he who fears the Lord returns to Him with his heart [6].

21.10.2.en: It is said of the blessings of rebuke: "Turn you at my reproof: behold, I will pour out my spirit unto you, I will make known my words unto you" (Prov 1:23). "My son, despise not the chastening of the Lord, neither hate His reproof" (Prov 3:11). "For the commandment is a lamp; and the law is light; and reproofs of instruction are the way of life" (Prov 6:23). "Rebuke a wise man, and he will love thee" (Prov 9:8). "Whoso loveth instruction loveth knowledge: but he that hateth reproof is brutish" (Prov 12:1). "Poverty and shame shall be to him that refuseth instruction: but he that regardeth reproof shall be honoured" (Prov 13:18). "A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent" (Prov 15:5).

21.11.0.en: v It often happens that a man breaks down for a time when he is rebuked, and he resists and struggles. But afterward, in his solitude, where there is none but God and himself, he is not afraid of the displeasure of others, so he corrects himself; rather he fears the wrath of God for refusing correction. So he does not again repeat this conduct which his brother disapproved, and he loves his brother, whom he used to regard as an enemy while he was in sin, as much as he hates the sin itself [12].

21.11.1.en: St. Augustine The one mighty in speech is known from afar, but the prudent man is known when he slips [7].

21.11.2.en: Ben Sira distinguishes between him who has been given the power of speech and him who enjoys prudence; the first is occupied with his reputation and fame, while the second is occupied with the salvation of his soul, so he realizes his sins and confesses them, returning to God in repentance.

21.11.3.en: He who builds his house with other men's money is like one who gathers his stones in a storm (or for his tomb) [8].

21.11.4.en: Among Ben Sira's counsels is his concern for managing financial matters wisely; therefore he warns against taking loans beyond a man's ability and means in order to build his house.

21.11.5.en: The assembly of the wicked is like a blazing bundle, and their end is a flame of fire [9].

21.11.6.en: Though the wicked care for being united together like a bundle, it is kindled by the fires of evil, which burn and destroy. Here the wicked man often reaches the summit of his evil, and it is not enough for him to practice evil and boast of it and love it more than good, but he loves the wicked in order to share their evil with them or to urge them still more to practice it with all violence. His pleasure becomes the company of the wicked and consulting with them, for no purpose except that he is pleased by the destruction of men, and rejoices in deceit and lying.

21.11.7.en: The way of sinners is paved with stones, and at its end is the pit of Hades [10].

21.11.8.en: What is the way of sinners, paved with hard stones, and at its end the pit of Hades, but the broad way that leads to destruction (Mt 7:13)? As for the narrow way that leads to life (Mt 7:14), in it my soul sings: "I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me" (Gal 2:20).

21.11.9.en: v When a man practices unlawful things, he fears what he has done!

21.11.11.en: v The king came out to see those invited guests who had come, and he saw there a man clothed in filthy garments (Mt 22:11-13).

21.11.12.en: And he said to him: Tell me, friend, who let you in when you are not clothed in the glorious garments of the feast?

21.11.13.en: Why do you come here in these filthy garments? These garments do not befit the feast.

21.11.14.en: And the king commanded the servants, and they bound his hands, and tied his feet, and cast him into the fearful darkness.

21.12.0.en: Where there is great weeping and gnashing of teeth for that one clothed in filthy garments at the feast [13].

21.12.1.en: St. Mar Jacob of Serugh In the broad way I suffer the shame of nakedness, but in the narrow way I strip off the garments of the world and put on the garment of righteousness.

21.12.2.en: v The garment of righteousness was given to us formerly in Paradise, and we were stripped of it, and became naked. This nakedness of the prodigal son the father granted that it be covered, for he said at his return: "Bring him quickly the first robe" (see Lk 15:22).

21.12.3.en: The first robe is the garment of righteousness which man rightly received at his creation, but when he was deceived by the serpent he lost it. Again it is said of this nakedness: "Blessed is he that watcheth, and keepeth his garments, lest he walk naked" (Rev 16:15). For we keep our garments when we keep the commandments of righteousness in our hearts, so that even if we are stripped and appear naked before the Judge by iniquity, by repentance we are covered and the righteousness we lost returns to us.

21.13.s.en: 3. Flee from folly and seek wisdom

21.13.0.en: 12 He that keepeth the law of the Lord getteth the understanding thereof. 13 And the perfection of the fear of the Lord is wisdom. 14 He that is not clever will not be taught. 15 But there is a cleverness that aboundeth in bitterness. 16 The knowledge of a wise man shall abound like a flood, and his counsel is like a pure fountain of life. 17 The inner parts of a fool are like a broken vessel, and he will hold no knowledge as long as he liveth. 18 If a skilful man hear a wise word, he will commend it, and add unto it; but as soon as one of no understanding heareth it, it displeaseth him, and he casteth it behind his back. 19 The talking of a fool is like a burden in the way, but grace shall be found in the lips of the wise. 20 They inquire at the mouth of the prudent man in the congregation, and they shall ponder his words in their heart. 21 As is a house that is destroyed, so is wisdom to a fool; and the knowledge of the unwise is as talk without sense. 22 Instruction unto fools is as fetters on the feet, and like manacles on the right hand.

21.13.1.en: What occupies Ben Sira is the sanctification of the inner man, that the believer may enjoy the spirit of wisdom and discernment in all aspects of his life. Therefore he called us to seek the perfection of the fear of the Lord [11] and to enjoy true knowledge as a fountain of life overflowing upon the mind and the heart [13], and to enjoy divine grace [16], and to remove folly by acquiring wisdom [18], and to persevere in holy teaching as an ornament that adorns the soul [21], and so on.

21.13.2.en: He who keeps the Law has mastered his thoughts, and the perfection of the fear of the Lord is wisdom [11].

21.14.0.en: v The difference between wisdom and folly is like light compared with darkness; I think it is fitting that he used the comparison of light for the perception of goodness. And since darkness in its nature is not a reality (has no being)... whereas light can be perceived in its essence. By this comparison he showed that evil has no existence in itself, but consists in the lack of goodness, while goodness is always existing and abiding, and does not consist in the lack of anything higher than itself [14].

21.14.1.en: St. Gregory of Nyssa Between the traits of the wise man and the traits of the fool:

21.14.2.en: By the wonderful divine grace the folly of man is shattered and the wisdom of Christ shines forth in his mind and heart and words and conduct. Truly, what comparison is there between him whom the folly of the powers of darkness enslaves and him whom the wisdom of God incarnate frees?!

21.15.0.en: v The wise person and the foolish person have nothing in common, whether in the terms of human memorials or in divine rewards... The wise man will not share the fate of the fool [15].

21.15.1.en: St. Gregory the Wonderworker 1. He likens the mind of the fool to a broken vessel in which he keeps nothing [14], and the mind of the wise man to a fountain of sweet and pure water. 2. The fool is like a ruined house, in which nothing good dwells, but some wild beasts and birds dwell [18]. 3. The fool hears the word of God and spits it out, for he counts it an illogical word, unacceptable and without meaning. 4. The fool is like the simpleton; there are fetters on his feet and on his right hand, preventing him from moving and working [19]. 5. The fool laughs with a loud voice, and the wise man smiles in a stillness that reveals his peace and inward joy [20]. 6. Instruction is for the wise man like an ornament that adorns the heavenly bride and a bracelet on his arm that urges him to holy spiritual work [21]. 7. The fool enters the house of one he visits rashly, and the wise man waits for the master of the house to permit him to enter [22]. 8. The fool looks in from the door to see what is inside the house, but the well-mannered wise man stands outside! [23]. 9. It befits the wise man not to intrude on the privacy of others, so he does not eavesdrop on anyone [24]. 10. The wise man weighs his words, so no vain word comes out of his mouth, while the fool repeats his words [25]. 11. The minds of fools are in their mouths, but the mouths of the wise are in their minds; they utter no word without thinking about it.

21.15.2.en: He who is not clever is not taught, but there is a cleverness that increases bitterness [12].

21.15.3.en: Intelligence is a gift that God offers to men, but pride turns intelligence into bitterness.

21.15.4.en: The knowledge of the wise man is like a flood, and his counsel overflows abundantly like a fountain of life [13].

21.15.5.en: The wise man drinks his fill of true knowledge, and it gives him delight, and it overflows within him like a flood that cannot be measured. It also overflows upon his brethren in sincere counsel like a fountain of life. This is the work of the Holy Spirit in us (Mk 13:11).

21.15.6.en: The inner workings of the fool (his mind) are like a broken vessel, which retains nothing of knowledge [14].

21.15.7.en: Wisdom overflows upon man in his depths with knowledge like a flood that does not cease. But the fool is like a broken vessel that will keep nothing within it. Since folly begets evil, the fool suffers emptiness, and becomes like a dumb beast that dies and perishes as though he had never existed at some time. But the wise man, even if he dies, departs to Paradise to enjoy eternal glories and immortality.

21.16.0.en: v Insensibility and unreasonableness beget in the soul ignorance of God, and this ignorance begets evil. But the knowledge of God brings goodness and saves the soul. Therefore if you remain in a state of loftiness with knowledge of God and an effort not to satisfy your own lusts, your mind turns toward virtue. But if you are drunk with ignorance of God, and enjoy the satisfaction of your evil lusts, forgetting the afflictions that await you after death, you perish like the dumb beast [16].

21.16.1.en: St. Anthony the Great If a man of understanding hears a word of wisdom, he praises it and adds to it.

21.16.2.en: But the one immersed in pleasures, when he hears it, hates it and casts it behind his back [15].

21.16.3.en: How great the difference between the wise man who finds his delight in a word of wisdom and in continual growth in knowledge, and the fool, who cannot bear a word of wisdom, but makes light of it and hates it and ignores it, and counts it as depriving him of his happiness and his temporal pleasures.

21.16.4.en: The talk of a fool is like a heavy burden on a journey, but grace is on the lips of the prudent man [16].

21.16.5.en: How great the difference between the wise man and the fool: grace clings to the lips of the first, so no one tires of the words of grace that come from his mouth. But the talk of the fool is without benefit, and whoever accompanies him wishes not to hear his words, because they are heavy and corrupting.

21.17.0.en: They seek the utterance of the prudent man in the assembly, and ponder his words in their hearts [17].

21.17.1.en: When the wise man speaks in an assembly, all listen to him, because he instills delight in them and fills them with hope, and urges them to continual progress. They count every word he utters as having its benefit in the life of the hearer as in society.

21.17.2.en: The word "heart" here, as was previously indicated, means thought or mind. So the hearer of the wise man takes care to keep what he hears and to cherish it, and to ruminate on it continually!

21.18.0.en: Wisdom to the fool is like a vanished house, and the knowledge of the ignorant is talk that does not stand examination [18].

21.18.1.en: The fool finds the words of wisdom burdensome; he counts them as an illusion, or as a house in which he does not wish to dwell, indeed as a passing dream.

21.18.2.en: The day on which a man learns nothing new is not only lost from his life, but it spoils what he had learned before. It is as though man's knowledge will not be static; it either renews itself and grows, or stops, not to remain as it is, but loses its time, and his knowledge weakens, and he falls behind. St. Gregory likens it to one who swims in a sea: either he advances to the harbor or he stops in the middle of the sea, and so sinks and perishes.

21.19.0.en: Instruction to the fool is like fetters on the feet, and like a manacle on the right hand [19].

21.19.1.en: Instruction is very heavy to the fool, for he counts it as fetters on his life that deprive him of freedom in conduct and enjoyment.

21.20.s.en: 4. The manners of the wise man

21.20.0.en: 23 A fool lifteth up his voice with laughter; but a wise man doth scarce smile a little. 24 Learning is unto a wise man as an ornament of gold, and like a bracelet upon his right arm. 25 A fool's foot is soon in his neighbor's house; but a man of experience is ashamed of him. 26 A fool will peep in at the door into the house; but he that is well nurtured will stand without. 27 It is the rudeness of a man to hearken at the door; but a wise man will be grieved with the disgrace. 28 The lips of talkers will be telling such things as pertain not unto them; but the words of such as have understanding are weighed in the balance. 29 The heart of fools is in their mouth; but the mouth of the wise is in their heart.

21.20.1.en: Ben Sira presents to us some traits of the conduct of the wise man, such as the smile instead of laughing aloud [20], a special esteem for instruction, so that he treasures it as the bride treasures the ornaments and jewels that her bridegroom gives her [21}, not being hasty in entering the house of one of his relatives or friends [22], and not eavesdropping at the door [24], and not speaking too much [25], while weighing every word before uttering it [26].

21.20.2.en: The fool raises his voice in laughter, but the clever man smiles quietly with some hesitation [20].

21.20.3.en: v If we watch over ourselves with the fear of God when we enter the company of others, and if we care for our hearts in vigilance, we find no cause to be troubled or to laugh. For in the presence of the fear of God there is no one laughing. As for fools, it has been said that they raise their voice in laughter. The words of the fool carry disturbance, but the righteous man speaks only to smile [17].

21.20.4.en: v If before our encounters with others we prepare our hearts by watching in the fear of God, why should we find any reason to be disturbed or to laugh? In truth there is no one laughing in the presence of a godly fear. It is said of the foolish that they raise their voices when they laugh, and that the talk of the fool is disturbing and leads to the loss of delight. At any rate, it is said of the righteous man that he merely smiles. Therefore if we bring to ourselves the remembrance of God, and fill our thoughts with quiet humility when we are in the company of our friends, then we love them in this manner, and we set before our eyes the fearful judgment of God. For God dwells where there is quietness, gentleness and humility.

21.20.5.en: Sts. Barsanuphius and John St. Basil made clear the distinction between corrupting laughter and laughter in the sense of the soul's joy and exultation in God.

21.20.6.en: v Indulging in laughter in an uncontrolled and exaggerated way is a sign of excess and a lack of a man's control over his feelings, and a failure to suppress the soul's levity by using the mind firmly. It is not unseemly to bear witness to the soul's cheerfulness by a joyful smile, if only it illustrates what is written: "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance" (Prov 15:13). But hoarse laughter, with no control of the movements of the body, is no indication of a soul well ordered, or of personal dignity, or of one who rules himself.

21.20.7.en: This kind of laughter is condemned by the Preacher especially as destroying the steadiness of the soul, in the words: "I said of laughter, It is mad" (Eccl 2:2). Again: "For as the crackling of thorns under a pot, so is the laughter of the fool" (Eccl 7:6). Moreover, the Lord shows that He practiced these necessary emotions that are bound up with the body, as well as those connected with virtue, for example sorrow over the sorrowful and compassion for them, but as we know from the Gospel story He never laughed. On the contrary, He declared that those who give themselves up to laughter are unhappy (Lk 6:25).

21.20.8.en: Let us not allow the word (laughter) to deceive us, for it has two meanings. Holy Scripture often uses it of the joy of the spirit and the delight of the feelings that follows good works. For example Sarah says: "God hath made me to laugh" (Gen 21:6). And there is another saying: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh" (Lk 6:21). In a similar way the words of Job: "Till he fill thy mouth with laughing" (Job 8:21). All these witnesses of gladness point to the soul's cheerfulness instead of boisterous merriment. Therefore he who is master of every passion and feels no agitation in his enjoyment, or at least shows no outward expressions, but tends to control every harmful pleasure firmly, such a one is perfectly chaste, and in truth has clearly been freed from every sin [18].

21.20.9.en: St. Basil the Great Instruction is to the prudent man like an ornament of gold, and like a bracelet on his right arm [21].

21.20.10.en: The wise man rejoices in instruction, like the bride who treasures the gifts of her bridegroom that he gives her to adorn herself with.

21.20.11.en: The foot of the fool is quick in entering a house, but the man of wide experience stands outside with dignity [22].

21.20.12.en: The wise man moves with dignity and modesty, so he does not hasten to enter the houses of his friends, relying on his close friendship with them, but he knows the limits of friendship and does not transgress them.

21.20.13.en: He who lacks discernment stares from the door into the house, but the well-mannered man stands outside [23].

21.21.0.en: A man shows his lack of manners by eavesdropping at the door, and the prudent man is grieved by that fault [24].

21.22.0.en: The lips of fools describe matters in detail, and the words of the prudent are weighed in the balance [25].

21.23.0.en: The hearts of fools are in their mouths, and the mouths of the wise are in their hearts [26].

21.23.1.en: v For a good reason the prophet said: "The tongue (of the wicked) deviseth mischiefs" (Ps 52:4). Contemplation belongs to the living soul through its living feeling, but the tongue was not created as befits the rational nature, but to be a servant of the rational nature. Nevertheless another prophet shows a trustworthy, inspired and perfect saying, for he says: "The minds (hearts) of fools are in their mouths," meaning by this that they utter things at random with no foundation, for they are accustomed not to return to the consideration of the mind after meditating on it in the heart, but walk in a rash movement of the tongue with levity.

21.23.2.en: If the heart of the fool is in his mouth, it is because he does not speak what he thinks, but thinks after he speaks. This points to the tongue of the fool, but of the tongue of the wise man we read rather: "The mouth of the righteous speaketh wisdom" (Ps 37:30). "My tongue is the pen of a ready writer" (Ps 37:30). The tongue of the wise man is born of meditation on wisdom, therefore it is like the pen of a writer, which never speaks in confusion or with doubt. Rather it submits to what is thought and what is read, and so overflows with keen intelligence according to the judgment of the person [19].

21.24.0.en: 30 When the ungodly curseth Satan, he curseth his own soul. 31 A whisperer defileth his own soul, and is hated wheresoever he dwelleth.

21.24.1.en: If the wicked man curses Satan, he curses his own soul [27].

21.24.2.en: Some see that the speech here is about one who thinks that someone is a demon and curses him, for the curse returns upon himself. The scholar Origen ascribes every demon to a particular sin, so he who commits many sins is like that man who dwelt in the tombs and in whom a legion dwelt, that is, many demons (Mk 5:9; Lk 8:30).

21.24.3.en: v If Satan is called "the adversary," then all who are against the will of God can be called devils [20].

21.24.4.en: v Why does it seem strange that we ascribe a demon to every kind of sin, when it is written that a legion of demons was found in one person? Indeed I recall a similar saying in our interpretation of the passage in a psalm: "I will early destroy all the wicked of the land; that I may cut off all wicked doers from the city of the Lord" (Ps 101:8). It is also said: "a two-edged sword in the hand of the righteous" (see 149:6), without doubt it is used to shatter the opposing powers. But I think that in order to give a stronger and decisive confirmation we cite the word of the Apostle Paul: "And the God of peace shall bruise Satan under your feet shortly" (Rom 16:20) [21].

21.24.5.en: The scholar Origen The slanderer defiles his own soul, and his neighbors will hate him [28].

21.24.6.en: The slanderer does not harm others as much as he harms himself. It is reported of St. Augustine that he wrote two lines of verse against slander and hung them in the dining room. It happened that some bishops sat with him at table and began to speak ill of certain people, so he advised them, saying: Either you erase these two lines, or I will rise from the table.

21.24.7.en: v The man who does not know how to distinguish between good and evil has no right to judge men that this one is good and that one is wicked. He who knows God is good. And if a man is not good, this means that he does not know God and God does not know him. For goodness is the only means of knowing God [22].

21.24.8.en: St. Anthony the Great v If you hear someone reviling another, flee from him as you would flee from a poisonous serpent, until he is ashamed and learns not to speak this way again.

21.25.s.en: To You I flee, O Savior of the fallen

21.25.0.en: v Your commandment is a wonderful light and a blazing fire, revealing my sins and kindling my heart with the fires of Your love.

21.25.1.en: The serpent crawls to bite me with its deadly venom, and roars like a lion to terrify me in the wilderness of this world.

21.25.2.en: To whom shall I flee but to You, O Forgiver of sins, and Giver of joyful hope and righteousness and holiness.

21.25.3.en: v Your commandment lifts me out of hatred and violence and injustice; so I cling to You and acquire Your love and compassion and humility.

21.25.4.en: I will not forget that I am dust and ashes, and corruption has crept into me, but You embrace me, You who raise those who are going down, and save the fallen, and establish those who stand, and lift the earthly as to Your heavens.

21.25.5.en: v You discipline me with Your rebuke to me, so I feel Your love, and return to You.

21.25.6.en: You grant me Your wisdom, so I do not build my house on the sand of the world, but dwell in You, O Rock of eternity.

21.25.7.en: I cling to those who give thanks to You, and I do not sit in the assembly of the wicked.

21.25.8.en: Let not the broad way of sinners draw me, but I delight in being crucified with You, O Way, Truth and Life.

21.25.9.en: v Your commandments are in their essence a call to possess You, O Word of God.

21.25.10.en: Do not cease to say: "I am..." that I may know You and possess You.

21.25.11.en: In You I enjoy wisdom and discernment, and shake off folly and ignorance.

21.25.12.en: In You I walk in the light, and I hear Your wonderful voice: "Ye are the light of the world" (Mt 5:14).

21.25.13.en: The frail darkness of sin is scattered, and it has no inward place!

21.25.14.en: I thank You, for in my folly I was like a broken vessel that does not keep the water of life, and in You I enjoy a fountain of sweet and pure water.

21.25.15.en: In my folly I was like a ruined house, inhabited by the powers of darkness like wild beasts and birds, and in You I enjoy Your Kingdom within me.

21.25.16.en: In my folly I mocked Your word, and in You I sing:

21.25.17.en: "How sweet are thy words unto my taste! yea, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" (Ps 119:103).

21.25.18.en: In my folly I used to laugh with an empty loud voice, and in You my smile proclaims Your dwelling in me.

21.25.19.en: In my folly I thought Your commandments fetters and a heavy yoke, and in You I see them as the precious ornament that the heavenly bride treasures.

21.25.20.en: In my folly I was rash in everything, and in You I go forward in quietness as from glory to glory.

21.25.21.en: v Grant me to find the word of wisdom sweet, and to count it a pearl that I keep in my mind and heart.

21.25.22.en: I ruminate on it continually, and reckon that I have not yet reached its depths.

21.25.23.en: Remove from me folly and chatter, that my words may not be a burden to those who hear them.

21.25.24.en: Grant me Your grace, that I may embrace Your wisdom; fill me with true delight, and let everyone I meet long to possess it and practice it.

21.25.25.en: Let him contemplate it from time to time, as he tastes its sweetness in his depths.

21.25.26.en: v Train me to imitate You, O my Creator and Savior.

21.25.27.en: I am the work of Your hands, indebted to You for all my life.

21.25.28.en: You ask me continually: "Wilt thou be made whole?" Teach me not to press upon any of my brethren, nor to break into his dwelling without asking his permission.

21.25.29.en: Sanctify my steps and my words, that I may feel Your company with me in every breath of my life.

21.25.30.en: Remove from me vain chatter, and guard my tongue from slander.
